source_metadata.title: Generative design of bacteriophages with genome language models
source_metadata.source_type: primary research article; computational generative genomics and experimental synthetic biology
source_metadata.supplementary_note: The primary article points to supplementary Materials and Methods, Supplementary Text, Figs. S1-S30, Table S1, MDAR checklist, and Data S1; these were not used because the task specifies no supplementary source material.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study tested whether genome language models could generate complete, viable bacteriophage genomes with specified host tropism using ΦX174 and Escherichia coli C as the design template and target host.
The design template was ΦX174, a lytic Microviridae phage with an approximately 5.4-kb genome containing 11 genes, at least seven regulatory elements, and two recognition sequences.

The full design pipeline combined Evo 1 and Evo 2 pretraining, task-specific fine-tuning on Microviridae genomes, ΦX174-specific prompt engineering, inference-time guidance using genomic-architecture and host-tropism predictors, computational filtering, DNA synthesis, and experimental validation.
Evo 1 and Evo 2 had been pretrained on large DNA corpora that included more than 2 million bacteriophage genomes.

Natural phage sequences were classified as viral by geNomad at rates of 89% to 100% depending on viral realm, whereas randomly scrambled natural phage sequences were classified as viral at rates of 1.9% to 11%.
Across viral-realm prompts, 19% to 33% of Evo 1 generations and 34% to 38% of Evo 2 generations were classified as viral by geNomad.
Generated sequences had low nucleotide similarity to natural sequences but retained phage-like coding density, predicted protein structure confidence, and functional annotation profiles.
The authors concluded that pretrained Evo models can generate biologically realistic phage-like genomic sequences while introducing diversity beyond observed natural evolution.
Evo 1 7B 131K and Evo 2 7B 8K were fine-tuned on approximately 15,000 Microviridae sequences to improve modeling of ΦX174-like genomes.

The generation strategy used short prefixes from the conserved start of ΦX174-like genomes; the fine-tuned models could recall ΦX174-like sequences, whereas the base models failed to recall ΦX174 across tested prompt lengths.

Sequence-quality constraints excluded nonnucleotide characters, restricted genome length to 4-6 kb and GC content to 30-65%, excluded DNA homopolymers longer than 10 bases, and required at least seven predicted protein hits to natural phage proteins.
The host-tropism constraint required generated spike proteins to have at least 60% sequence identity to the ΦX174 spike protein.

Diversification filters favored proteomes with no more than 95% average amino acid identity to natural proteins and used gene-architecture, gene-count, and synteny constraints to permit controlled departures from ΦX174.
After tropism filtering, the maximum retained fraction was 100% for Evo 1 SFT generations.

atoms.canonical_statement: Diverse ΦX174-like generation required balancing prompt length and sampling temperature: prompts of about 4-9 nucleotides and temperatures of about 0.7-0.9 were used to avoid both memorized recall and insufficient conditioning.
Sequence diversity increased with prompt length and sampling temperature after tropism filtering without eliminating a high fraction of sequences during later diversification filtering.

The experimental candidate set comprised 302 generated phage genomes selected after computational filtering; candidates spanned 4-6 kb, had average amino acid identities to natural proteins as low as 63%, and largely retained spike-protein identity above 85%.

CheckV classified more than 87% of the generated candidate sequences as High Quality or Complete, and most candidates had greater than 40% nucleotide identity to ΦX174 and Microviridae training genomes.

Experimental validation used in vitro assembly of circular double-stranded DNA genome products, transformation into E. coli C, high-throughput growth inhibition screening, propagation, titration, PCR, and long-read sequencing.
The investigators successfully synthesized and assembled 285 of 302 generated genomes; the other 17 failed because of high-complexity DNA synthesis.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that genome language models combined with inference-time steering and filtering can design viable phage genomes with high specificity for the intended bacterial host.

The 16 viable generated phages contained hundreds of synonymous, nonsynonymous, noncoding, and insertion/deletion differences relative to their nearest natural genomes and included gene insertions, losses, truncations, elongations, and gene swapping events.
Relative to their nearest natural genomes, generated phages had overall sequence similarities of 93.2% to 98.8%.
Relative to their nearest natural genomes, generated phages contained 49-143 synonymous substitutions, 14-51 nonsynonymous substitutions, 0-3 indels, and 0-12 intergenic substitutions.
Among generated phage genomes with fewer than 25 nonsynonymous mutations, 3 of 5 tested designs were viable, corresponding to 60.0%.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors estimated an expected survival rate of only 2.3% for generated genomes with fewer than 25 nonsynonymous mutations and approximately 0% for higher mutational burdens under a null model based on prior ΦX174 mutation lethality, substantially below observed survival.

Mutations in 13 generated phages could not be recapitulated from known natural sequences; targeted deletions showed that some generated noncoding insertions were essential in their specific genome context.

Evo-Φ36 replaced the ΦX174-like DNA-packaging protein J with a shorter homolog resembling the distant phage G4; the generated genome was viable even though prior work found that swapping G4 J directly into ΦX174 was nonviable.
Evo-Φ36 shared 97.1% sequence similarity with ΦX174, whereas phage G4 shared 63.0%; the G4-like J protein was 25 amino acids long compared with 38 amino acids for the ΦX174 J protein.
The Evo-Φ36 J protein was viable in the natural phage NC51 but remained lethal in ΦX174, indicating that genome context altered compatibility of the packaging protein.
Cryo-electron microscopy resolved ΦX174 at 2.8 Å and Evo-Φ36 at 2.9 Å, enabling comparison of capsid and J-protein interactions.

The authors interpreted the Evo-Φ36 structural results as evidence that generative design can discover coevolutionary sequence solutions that preserve compatible capsid-packaging interactions in divergent genome contexts.
Individual lysis phenotypes were quantified using steepest decline in host OD600, minimum OD600 after infection, and time to minimum OD600; 16 natural ΦX174-like phages were rebooted as comparators.

Generated phages showed a broader range of lysis phenotypes than natural ΦX174-like comparators; Evo-Φ2483, Evo-Φ69, Evo-Φ108, and Evo-Φ111 had strong lytic phenotypes, whereas Evo-Φ63 was among the slowest and shallowest.
Relative fitness was tested by coinfecting E. coli C with all 16 generated phages plus ΦX174 at equal multiplicity of infection and tracking each phage by sequencing over six hours.
Evo-Φ69, Evo-Φ100, and Evo-Φ111 outcompeted other phages in pooled infection, and Evo-Φ69 reached cumulative fold changes of approximately 10-fold to 41-fold after six hours.
The area-under-the-curve competition metric showed Evo-Φ69 significantly outcompeted ΦX174 and other generated phages, with Tukey-adjusted P < 0.0001.

concept.text: Competition fitness by cumulative log2 fold-change AUC

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors reported no correlation between sequence naturalness and relative competitiveness among generated phages.

Two ΦX174-resistant E. coli C strains, CR1 and CR2, were evolved; CR1 carried a waaT L259W missense mutation and CR2 carried a single-base deletion at waaT nucleotide 485 that produced a premature stop codon.

Resistance challenge experiments compared ΦX174 alone, a natural cocktail of 16 ΦX174-like phages plus ΦX174, and a generated cocktail of all 16 generated phages plus ΦX174 across susceptible, resistant, and mixed E. coli C cultures with serial passage.
The generated phage cocktail inhibited resistant strain CR1 after one passage and sustained growth inhibition for at least five passages.

atoms.canonical_statement: ΦX174 alone and the natural ΦX174-like phage cocktail failed to inhibit either resistant strain after five serial passages.

The predominant counter-resistant phages Evo-ΦR1 and Evo-ΦR2 could be reconstructed largely from segments of generated parent phages plus only a small number of newly acquired SNVs, consistent with recombination and mutation during passage.
Across the capsid and spike proteins of Evo-ΦR1 and Evo-ΦR2, 15 nonsynonymous mutations relative to ΦX174 were observed, 14 of which had already been generated by Evo.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that sequence diversity introduced by Evo likely contributed to the generated phage cocktail’s ability to adapt to bacterial resistance and may support more resilient phage therapies.

The authors state that this work achieved the first generative design of complete bacteriophage genomes and demonstrated a controllable genome-design framework that produced 16 viable, genomically diverse phages from nearly 300 experimentally tested designs.

Examples highlighted in the discussion included Evo-Φ36 with a contextually functional truncated J gene, Evo-Φ63 with a genome 5% (268 nucleotides) longer than ΦX174, Evo-Φ69 with strong pooled-competition fitness, and Evo-Φ2483 with fast lysis.
The authors state that further bacteriophage genome-design progress will require additional methodological innovations and improved training datasets.
The authors identify cost-effective DNA synthesis and assembly as particular challenges for extending the approach to larger phage genomes.

The authors explicitly note that AI generation of new phage genomes raises biosafety, biocontainment, and biosecurity considerations and recommend involvement of safety and security professionals throughout future project lifecycles.

The authors report that experiments were conducted at the biosafety level appropriate for bacteriophages and nonpathogenic bacterial hosts with supplementary precautions; the detailed procedures are located in supplementary materials.

The final conclusion is that generative AI captured evolutionary constraints with enough fidelity to produce viable complete bacteriophage genomes, while broader generalization to larger and more complex genomes remains a future direction.

Brian L. Hie reported outside interests in Arpelos Biosciences and Genyro as a scientific cofounder; Samuel H. King and Brian L. Hie were named inventors on a provisional patent application covering generative bacteriophage genome design methods; the other authors declared no competing interests.

The article reports public availability of Microviridae training datasets, Evo 1/Evo 2 generation and fine-tuning code, phage genome design/analysis code, fine-tuned models, annotated generated phage genomes in GenBank, and ΦX174/Evo-Φ36 cryo-EM maps and structures in EMDB/PDB.
